title: The Cure for the Vibe Coding Hangover — Corey J. Gallon, Rexmore

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk presents a structured framework for building production software with AI coding agents, covering planning, implementation loops, and tooling. The framework is designed for coding assistants and developer platforms, targeting engineers building real-world applications with AI agents. The framework has been applied across teams from solo shops to Fortune 500 companies for production software development. Requires programming experience and willingness to adopt structured planning, targeting engineers dissatisfied with ad-hoc vibe coding. A practical three-pillar framework of Principles, Process, and Tools distilled from years of applied engineering work. summary: Corey J. Gallon introduces the "vibe coding hangover"—the despair following brittle, unmaintainable demoware built through low-spec, zero-planning AI coding agent usage. The cure is a practical framework with three pillars: Principles (philosophy), Process (workflow), and Tools (accelerators). Ten principles span general (accelerated learning, architect-implementer boundary, slow down to go fast), planning (specification over prompt engineering, define done, feature atomicity, dependency-driven development), and implementation (one atomic feature at a time, context engineering, make it work first). The Process phase operationalizes principles in two stages: planning and implementation. Planning is purely the engineer's work, transforming a vague project idea into atomic, sequenced, fully specified features through five sequential steps: Vision, Features, Specification, Dependencies, and Plan. Vision capture produces a master project specification. Feature identification extracts and categorizes all functionality into a feature inventory with unique IDs and complexity estimates. Iterative specification development transforms each feature through three-level refinement for both implementation and validation contracts. Dependency analysis synthesizes scattered declarations into a validated dependency matrix and visual graph, resolving circular dependencies through elimination, revised specification, feature splitting, or consolidation. Implementation plan development uses topological sort to organize features into dependency-ordered phases with binary validation gates and critical path identification. Implementation is a tight rapid loop executed per atomic feature, starting with context assembly that curates only relevant planning artifacts per feature. The implementation loop itself—where the AI writes code—follows four steps: write code from technical contracts, execute and sense via three digital sensors (visual, auditory, tactile), test and validate against the validation contract, and correlate all signals to diagnose what failed and why. The loop continues until all tests pass and all sensors report clean execution, at which point the agent creates an atomic git commit. Tools comprise four foundational capabilities: a coding environment (AI agent, execution sandbox, IDE/editor, voice input), a multisensory feedback system (visual, auditory, tactile sensor tools), context engineering and assembly tools (cross-referencing, slash commands, templates, markdown), and version control with progress tracking (git plus the implementation plan as a living progress tracker).
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The Vibe Coding Hangover
sections.summary: Opens with the narrative of vibe coding: inspiration strikes, the AI agent builds working code, but when you return to maintain or extend it, you realize you don't understand it and must throw it away. Defines vibe coding as low-spec, zero-planning AI development producing brittle, unmaintainable demoware, with the hangover being the resulting despair.

sections.title: Introduction and Audience
sections.summary: Describes who will enjoy the talk: engineers valuing programming as learning, wanting to own software, wanting to be bosses of agents not confused interns, sick of throwing away code. Notes the talk is not for those satisfied with AI doing work without understanding. Introduces Corey's background: AI-native holding company, building coding agents since 2022, coffee nerd, pickleball fanatic.

sections.title: Framework Overview
sections.summary: The framework comprises three pillars: Principles (philosophy), Process (workflow), and Tools (accelerators/enablers reflecting principles). Framework is adaptive to all software types. Examples of production software built with this approach include litigation support, appliance monitoring, and digital publishing systems.

sections.title: Principles - General
sections.summary: Three general principles: (1) AI engineering is accelerated learning—every step creates learning opportunities so you build yourself, not just software; (2) You are the architect, agent is the implementer—own thinking, delegate doing; (3) Slow down and iterate to go fast—deliberate iteration enables compounding returns.

sections.title: Principles - Planning
sections.summary: Four planning principles: (1) Specification far exceeds prompt engineering; (2) Define done before implementing via executable tests and observable success criteria; (3) Feature atomicity—decompose features to irreducible tasks; (4) Dependency-driven development—schedule implementation by understanding feature relationships.

sections.title: Principles - Implementation
sections.summary: Three implementation principles: (1) Implement one atomic feature at a time with sequential focus, study, validation, and commit checkpoints; (2) Context engineering—curate context from persistent documents; (3) Make it work first, then make it right, then make it fast—build, learn, improve.

sections.title: Process Overview
sections.summary: The process puts principles into action with two distinct phases: planning (architectural thinking to define what to build) and implementation (agent executes specifications with oversight and validation). Planning produces artifacts enabling autonomous agent implementation; implementation uses those artifacts to build working software feature by feature.

sections.title: Process - Planning Step 1: Vision Capture
sections.summary: Transforms vague project ideas into a complete master project specification covering five sections: project purpose, essential functionality (3-5 core workflows), scope boundaries (now/next), technical context, and workflow details. Engineer thinks out loud with agent as thinking partner but makes all decisions. Output becomes foundation for feature extraction.

sections.title: Process - Planning Step 2: Feature Identification and Categorization
sections.summary: Systematically extracts all functionality units from the master project specification using targeted extraction questions per section. Builds raw feature list, analyzes natural groupings (3-7 categories), assigns unique feature IDs (e.g., core-001, api-101), and estimates complexity. Output is a complete categorized feature inventory traceable to source sections.

sections.title: Process - Planning Step 3: Iterative Specification Development
sections.summary: Transforms each feature from inventory into complete atomic implementation-ready specification using three-level refinement. Implementation contracts progress from plain English to logic flow to formal interfaces. Validation contracts progress from plain English scenarios to given-when-then test logic to formal test definitions. Atomicity is validated—if a feature spans multiple capabilities, it is split. Explicit binary dependencies are documented. Output is complete atomic feature specifications for every feature.

sections.title: Process - Planning Step 4: Dependency Analysis
sections.summary: Synthesizes scattered dependency declarations from individual feature specifications into a unified validated dependency matrix and visual graph. Process: extract matrix (row-by-row feature-to-feature grid), generate graph (nodes and edges via graphviz/mermaid), validate and clean via binary dependency test, detect cycles. Circular dependencies resolved through four strategies: dependency elimination, revised specification, feature splitting, or consolidation as last resort. Iterate until zero cycles remain. Outputs: validated dependency matrix with clear implementation layers and dependency graph showing structure.

sections.title: Process - Planning Step 5: Implementation Plan Development
sections.summary: Transforms validated dependency matrix into phased implementation roadmap. Topological sort organizes features into phases by dependency depth (no-dependency features = phase one, etc.). Verifies no intra-phase dependencies. Identifies critical path (longest dependency chain). Defines binary success criteria per phase, phase gates, task assignment guidance for agents, blocker management process, and progress tracking at feature/phase/critical-path levels. Output: comprehensive phased execution strategy enabling autonomous agent implementation.

sections.title: Process - Implementation: Multisensory Feedback Loop
sections.summary: Introduces the multisensory feedback loop as a key framework idea. The agent implements code, executes it, and gathers feedback through digital senses: visual (what renders), auditory (what system reports), tactile (how interactions respond). By correlating sensory feedback with formal test results, the agent understands both what failed (tests) and why (sensors). Loop continues until all acceptance criteria pass and all sensors report clean.

sections.title: Process - Implementation: Context Assembly
sections.summary: First step of implementation loop: curate planning artifacts into a focused context package per atomic feature. Four steps: (1) Feature specification assembly—include complete spec with at-referenced dependencies; (2) Dependency context gathering—pull in referenced dependency specifications and actual implemented code; (3) Implementation guidance—extract relevant plan sections; (4) Enable sensory capabilities—match acceptance criteria language to required sensory tools and at-reference reusable tool usage guides. Output is the curated context package—exactly what the agent needs. This is the only framework step where AI writes code.

sections.title: Process - Implementation: The Implementation Loop
sections.summary: The final implementation step transforms an atomic feature specification into working tested code via a tight four-step loop. (1) Write code—the agent implements following the feature's technical contracts, translating all three levels into working code. (2) Execute and sense—the agent runs the code and gathers comprehensive sensory feedback through visual, auditory, and tactile sensors based on acceptance criteria. (3) Test and validate—runs all validation contract test scenarios for binary pass/fail signals. (4) Correlate—the agent correlates signals across all sensors and test results; multiple sensors confirming the same issue validates diagnosis, conflicting signals reveal hidden complexity. The loop repeats until convergence: all tests pass and all sensors report clean. Then the agent creates an atomic git commit with structured message (feature ID, spec summary, validation confirmation, implementation notes). Output: a fully working, tested feature ready for integration.

sections.title: Tools - Foundational Capabilities Overview
sections.summary: The framework requires four foundational tool capabilities that enable the process: coding environment, multisensory feedback system, context engineering and assembly tools, and version control with progress tracking.

sections.title: Tools - Coding Environment
sections.summary: A complete development workspace supporting two simultaneous work types: architectural thinking/planning and autonomous agent implementation/testing. Four core components: (1) AI coding agent; (2) Execution sandbox—safe, isolated, disposable environment where agent code executes and tests run, providing freedom to experiment with easy reset and no failure consequences; (3) IDE or text editor (user preference); (4) Voice input—rapid speech-to-text capture at thinking speed, removing the typing bottleneck during exploratory planning work. Voice input is described as massively impactful.

sections.title: Tools - Multisensory Feedback System
sections.summary: Comprehensive validation infrastructure giving agents three digital sensors. Visual sense tools capture UI rendering (screenshots, layout, styling), system state (database contents, configuration, session data), and code structure—catching problems logs and tests miss. Auditory sense tools monitor logs (system narrating operations), errors and warnings (detected problems), API responses (intersystem communication), and stack traces (detailed failure information explaining why things fail). Tactile sensors enable active interaction testing: simulating user workflows end-to-end, API request-response cycles, performance validation, security checks, and integration testing—revealing behavior under actual use.

sections.title: Tools - Context Engineering and Assembly Tools
sections.summary: Systematic approach to assembling focused context packages through: (1) Cross-referencing system—declarative linking mechanism allowing documents to explicitly reference other documents, code files, or sections for automatic context assembly via dependency chains; (2) Slash commands—process automation triggering multi-step framework workflows through single invocation (context assembly, template instantiation, implementation session initialization); (3) Template system—structured document templates for every framework artifact (master project spec, feature spec, dependency matrix, implementation plan, implementation record) ensuring consistent format and completeness; (4) Markdown documentation—agents are highly literate in it, so tooling should rapidly convert any input to markdown.

sections.title: Tools - Version Control and Progress Tracking
sections.summary: Dual mechanism system: git for implementation history through atomic feature commits, and the implementation plan for feature completion tracking. Git shows what changed and when but not project state; the implementation plan fills that gap as a planning artifact that doubles as the progress tracker. Together they provide complete project provenance and current state visibility. The speaker notes this is the simplest form of project tracking and can be extended. A personal tool stack is shown but not discussed in detail.
